analysis.one_liner: Writes national passenger rights into aviation law, from delay explanations to medical kits on board.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 30 bipartisan cosponsors on the day it was introduced, but never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a set of national passenger rights into federal aviation law. Airlines would have had to explain flight delays and cancellations, show customers every fare they offer regardless of how the customer searches, stop charging fees for using only part of a ticket, keep emergency medical equipment on board, and let passengers off a plane stuck at the gate for over an hour. It also would have weakened the federal shield that blocks most state consumer laws from reaching airlines, and created a commission to study whether airline practices against travel agents and internet sellers were hurting consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers would gain concrete rights: an accurate explanation whenever a flight is delayed, canceled, or diverted; access to every fare an airline offers no matter how they search; the right to leave a plane stuck at the gate for more than an hour past departure; and minimum emergency medical and first-aid equipment on planes carrying at least 30 people [S2][S3]. Consumers would also benefit from the bill's finding that fewer travel agents and fewer independent price-comparison channels could leave shoppers with less information and higher prices [S3]. Travel agents and online fare distributors would gain from 90-day notice and 60-day cure rights before an airline cuts them off, and from a national commission charged with protecting consumer access to fare information [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Passengers would be entitled to an accurate explanation of the reasons for any flight delay, cancellation, or diversion, ending vague or no explanations from airlines.
Airlines could no longer hide fares from consumers or penalize people for using only part of a ticket, such as boarding only the return half of a round trip, or for buying one-way travel.
Passengers would have the right to exit an aircraft that has sat at the gate more than an hour past its scheduled departure when no clearance to leave is expected within 15 minutes.
The Secretary of Transportation would set minimum standards for resuscitation, emergency medical, and first-aid equipment on planes that carry at least 30 passengers.
The bill narrows federal preemption so states could regulate airline practices that do not directly set prices, routes, or service, opening airlines to state consumer-protection enforcement.

Ticket agents would get 90 days' written notice and 60 days to correct problems before losing their airline appointment, protecting an independent sales channel that the bill says keeps fare information in consumers' hands.

A 15-member National Commission would study and report on consumer access to fare and route information, airline reservation systems, and legal barriers distributors face in challenging anticompetitive airline practices.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines would bear the cost: new equipment purchases and crew training for medical kits, staffing and disclosure systems to explain delays and show full fares, forgone fees from hidden-city and partial-ticket penalties, and greater exposure to state consumer-protection lawsuits as federal preemption narrowed [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs fall on airlines, and airlines routinely pass operating costs into ticket prices, so consumers could pay somewhat higher fares for the required equipment, disclosure systems, and gate procedures.

The ticket-agent provisions primarily protect travel agencies, a business interest, and only indirectly help passengers; critics of such rules argue they preserve a middleman channel even as internet booking makes it less necessary.
Narrowing federal preemption could produce a patchwork of state consumer laws across the states an airline serves, which airlines argued raises legal costs and complicates a nationwide route network.
A large share of the bill's consumer-information agenda is delegated to a study commission, which produces recommendations rather than enforceable rules and can delay direct action for years.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are concrete and mostly cheap relative to airline revenues: truthful delay explanations, fare transparency, and a right to leave a stuck plane address real, well-known passenger frustrations, and medical-equipment standards are a straightforward safety measure. The costs are airline compliance expenses and some legal complexity from narrowed preemption, which likely show up partly in fares. The weakest part is the ticket-agent section, which is narrower industry relief than passenger protection, and the reliance on a study commission for the information-access question. On balance, the benefits to travelers outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Aviation Subcommittee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, never reaching a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 14, 1999 and referred the same day to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and to its Subcommittee on Aviation.

The bill text declares a national policy of basic consumer fair treatment and spells out specific airline practices that would count as unfair or deceptive, including withholding fare information and penalizing travelers for using part of a ticket.
No further action was ever taken on the bill, which never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
Thirty members cosponsored the bill, 19 Democrats and 11 Republicans, showing support from both parties at introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The airline industry. It avoided the new federal requirements on fare disclosure, delay explanations, gate-return rules, and on-board medical equipment, as well as the narrowed preemption that would have exposed it to state consumer laws.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 14, 1999 and sent it to its Aviation Subcommittee, where it received no further action

against.name: House Aviation Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan, with 19 of the 30 cosponsors Democrats and 11 Republicans; the bill never reached a vote where party lines could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed new federal mandates on airlines: fare disclosure, delay explanations, gate-return rights for stranded passengers, on-board medical equipment, and narrower preemption of state consumer laws. Every requirement is a cost or constraint the airlines would otherwise not have faced.

Travel agents would have gained 90-day written notice and 60 days to fix deficiencies before an airline could cut them off, plus a commission to study airline practices that squeeze independent distributors. The bill treats agents as a channel through which consumers learn about fares, so their survival is framed as a consumer-interest issue.

The bill would require airlines to give consumers full access to all fares regardless of the technology used to find them, and directs the new commission to examine internet-based fare comparison and the anticompetitive pressures airlines place on distributors.
